processing: Fresh leaf is pan-fired in a tilted cauldron heated above 300°C, turned by hand to prevent scorching, then rolled and shaped. It dries into a curved, rounded form.
harvest_season: Typically spring, with the first flush most valued, as with other Japanese green teas.
appearance_dry: Curved, rounded leaf, unlike the straight needles of steamed sencha.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear golden-yellow, as with other pan-fired greens.
appearance_wet: Typically whole, soft green leaves, less broken than deep-steamed tea.
taste_profile: Typically clean and lightly toasty, with the pan-fired aroma (kamaka) prized in this style in place of the marine depth of steamed tea.

brewing.notes: Pan-fired tea takes hotter water than sencha. Measures are a general starting point for the class.

vintage_note: As with other Japanese green teas, it is normally sold as the current year's crop, with first-flush lots the prize. Drink it within the year while the pan-fired aroma is fresh.
description:
Most Japanese green tea is steamed. This one is fired in a hot iron pan, and that puts it closer in spirit to Chinese green tea. Ureshino in Saga keeps a recognisable style of its own, using a tilted cauldron.

The leaf meets a pan above 300°C and is worked by hand so that it does not scorch, then rolled. The finished leaf is curved and rounded. The other main Japanese style, Aoyagi from Kumamoto and Miyazaki, uses a level pan.

The usual appeal of this class is a clean cup and a toasty aroma, and hotter water suits it better than sencha temperatures. If you normally brew Japanese greens at 70°C, try this one hotter before you judge it.

Don't confuse it with Ureshino's better-known steamed tamaryokucha, the rounded steamed style from the same town. On a label, look for 釜炒り and the maker's name.
history:
Tradition holds that in 1504 a Ming potter, 紅令民, brought a Nanjing pan to the area and taught the pan-firing method. That is a local account and not a documented fact: a 2017 study of tilted-pan firing notes that its origins remain partly unclear and written records of the method are scarce.

The same study, based on interviews about pre-mechanised work in Ureshino, found the steps close to those in the Chinese text 茶箋 and the late 17th-century Japanese farming manual 農業全書.
